en: The Noble Sūtra on Impermanence. Om, homage to the Omniscient One!

Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with a great community of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty monks.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, unstable, unreliable, and subject to change.
Therefore, monks, it is enough to turn away from all conditioned phenomena; it is enough to become dispassionate toward them; it is enough to be liberated from them."
For all beings, for all creatures, for all living things, life indeed ends with death; death is its finality. There is no such thing as non-death for one who is born.

Even those householders, monks—those from great *śāla* clans of brahmins, from great *śāla* clans of kṣatriyas, or from great *śāla* clans—who possess vast wealth and great enjoyments, and who have abundant collections of gems, rubies, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, gold, and silver—even they [must face this].

Those who possess vast accumulations of wealth, grain, treasuries, and storehouses; who have many female and male slaves, laborers, and servants; and who have many friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations—even for them, life ends in death and concludes in death. There is no such thing as non-death for one who is born. Furthermore, O monks, even those kings who are Kṣatriyas consecrated on the head, who have attained sovereignty, power, and heroism over the countryside, and who dwell having conquered a great circle of the earth—[for them too, life ends in death].
For even their life ends in death; death is its finality. There is no non-death for one who is born.

Even those monks, O bhikṣus, who are seers dwelling in the forest, subsisting on fallen fruit, eating fallen fruit, and maintaining themselves with fallen fruit—even for them, life ends in death; death is its finality.
There is no non-death for one who is born.

Furthermore, monks, even those gods of the desire realm—the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods—even for them, life ends in death; death is its finality. There is no such thing as non-death for one who is born. Furthermore, monks, even those form-realm gods who have attained the first dhyāna—the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā gods—[share this same fate].

For those who have attained the second dhyāna— the Parīttābhas, Apramāṇābhas, and Ābhāsvaras— and for those who have attained the third dhyāna— the Parīttaśubhas, Apramāṇaśubhas, and Śubhakṛtsnas— as well as for those who have attained the fourth dhyāna— the Anabhrakas, Puṇyaprasavas, Bṛhatphalas, Avṛhas, Atapas, Sudṛśas, Sudarśanas, and Akaniṣṭha devas— even for them, life ends in death; their existence culminates in death.
There is no end for that which is born; there is no living without dying.

Even those monks who are formless gods—those who have reached the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—even for them, life ends in death; death is the finality.
There is no immortality for one who is born;
such is this triple world.

Even those monks who are arhats, whose taints are exhausted, who have accomplished their task, performed what was to be done, laid down the burden, and attained their own goal—[even they are not exempt].

Even for those whose fetters of existence are completely exhausted, whose minds are well-liberated through right knowledge, and who have attained the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states— their bodies are likewise subject to the law of casting off.

And as for those monks who are Pratyekabuddhas, like the solitary rhinoceros horn, who tame themselves alone, pacify themselves alone, and attain final nirvana by themselves— their bodies, too, are subject to this law of casting off.

Monks, even for those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones who possess the power of the ten strengths, who are sublime seers, who roar the perfect lion’s roar, and who have ascended to the fearlessnesses of the four grounds of self-confidence—the fearlessness in proclaiming all dharmas, the fearlessness in leading others onto the path to Nirvāṇa, and the fearlessness in the knowledge that has abandoned the outflows—even for them, this body is subject to the law of casting off.
Their bodies are clear, firm, and as compact as the Nārāyaṇa-strength. Yet, even for them, this body is of a nature to be laid down.

Just as, monks, vessels made by a potter—whether unbaked or baked—are destined for breaking and end in breaking, even so, monks, for all beings, for all creatures, for all living things, life ends with death;
it terminates in death. There is no non-death for one who is born.

The Blessed One said this; having spoken thus, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke: "Impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena, subject to the nature of arising and passing away. Having arisen, they cease; their subsiding is bliss."
Just as a clay vessel made by a potter ends inevitably in breakage, so too does the life of sentient beings end in death.
Just as ripe fruits are constantly in danger of falling,
so too are sentient beings born of conditioned formations always in fear of death.
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall;
all unions end in separation; indeed, life ends in death.
The Blessed One spoke thus, and the monks and that entire assembly, being uplifted, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
Thus ends the Noble Sūtra on Impermanence.
